49007:
The learner's notes make a second point: some words and textures cannot carry their full essence into another language. This is true. Hebrew loves wordplay. God forms the human (*adam*) from the ground (*adamah*) (Gen 2:7). Amos sees a basket of summer fruit (*qayits*) and hears that the end (*qets*) has come (Amos 8:1-2). Jeremiah sees an almond branch (*shaqed*) and God says he is watching (*shoqed*) over his word (Jer 1:11-12). In English the connection disappears.

In John 3, Jesus tells Nicodemus he must be born *anōthen*, a Greek word that can mean "again" or "from above". Nicodemus hears "again" and asks how a man can re-enter his mother's womb (John 3:3-4). Jesus means "from above", by the Spirit. A few verses later, the same word *pneuma* means both "wind" and "Spirit" (John 3:8). No single English word can hold both senses. Some words are so rich that no translation word fits: Hebrew *hesed* is rendered "mercy", "lovingkindness", "steadfast love" or "loyal love" (Ps 136:1), and Greek *pistis* can mean faith, trust or faithfulness.

This is why translators must interpret. Some translations stay close to the original words (formal equivalence, like the KJV, ESV or NASB); others aim to carry the meaning in natural language (functional or dynamic equivalence, like the NLT). Each choice gains something and loses something. The best habit is to compare several translations, learn a few key words, and use good study notes. Lesson 4 covers translation in depth.
49008: Building the context of a passage
49009: Walk through these questions before deciding what a passage means for you.
49011: What do we know about the author, his situation and his relationship to the readers? Paul writing from prison sounds different from Paul planning a visit.
49013: Who first heard it? Israel in exile, a mixed Jewish-Gentile church, a persecuted congregation? What did they already know?
49015: What was happening in the world at the time? Which empire ruled? Is the date debated, and how would each date change the reading?
49017: What problem or purpose made the writer write? Look for statements of purpose.
49019: Story, law, poem, proverb, prophecy, letter, vision? Each genre has its own rules.
49021: Which customs and values are assumed: honour and shame, patronage, kinship, covenant, the ancient picture of the world?
49022: Then: what does it say to us?
49023: Having stood with the first hearers, ask what the same God is saying to us now, in light of Jesus.
49024: Hearing the Prodigal Son: a modern reader and a first hearer
49025: Luke 15:11-32 as many modern readers hear it and as a first-century village audience may have heard it. Several cultural details come from Kenneth Bailey's work; some (such as whether asking for the inheritance meant wishing the father dead) are debated by scholars like Amy-Jill Levine.
49027: A first hearer would likely hear
49029: A story told to people who need to be saved
49030: A story told because religious leaders complained that Jesus ate with sinners
49033: A shocking request that dishonours the father in front of the village
49036: An older man of honour running in public: he takes the shame on himself to reach his son first
49039: Full restoration of family status: the son is not a servant but a son
49042: A feast big enough for the whole village: public reconciliation
49045: The real target: the father goes out to him too, and the story ends without telling us whether he comes in
49046: John 3:3: born again or born from above?
49047: One Greek word with two senses, and how translations handle it.
49048: Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
49049: Takes *anōthen* as "again", which matches Nicodemus' reply in John 3:4.
49050: No one can see the kingdom of God without being born from above.
49051: Takes *anōthen* as "from above", matching John 3:31 where the same word means from above. A footnote gives "anew".
49052: No one can see the kingdom of God unless they are born again.
49053: Keeps "again" in the text and gives "from above" in a footnote, showing the translators knew both senses.
49055: Unless someone is born again / from above, he is not able to see the kingdom of God.
49056: Many scholars think John intends both senses: Nicodemus hears one, Jesus means the deeper one. No English word carries both.
49057: The Old Testament was written for us, but not to us.
49058: a principle Walton repeats across his work, e.g. *Wisdom for Faithful Reading* (2023); the title of his 2020 Festschrift, *For Us, but Not to Us*, comes from it
49060: Craig Keener (*IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament*), John Walton, Victor Matthews and Mark Chavalas (*IVP Bible Background Commentary: Old Testament*); most evangelical scholarship
49061: Recover the historical, cultural and linguistic setting of each text so that we hear what the first audience heard, then apply the same message today.
49062: It clears up many puzzles, guards against reading modern ideas into ancient texts, and respects God's choice to speak in history.
49063: Background can become a new expert key that ordinary readers cannot use. Scholars warn of "parallelomania" (Samuel Sandmel's word, 1962) — finding parallels everywhere and over-reading them.
49065: Bruce Malina, Jerome Neyrey, David deSilva, Kenneth Bailey
49066: Use models from cultural anthropology — honour and shame, patronage, kinship, purity — to understand the social world assumed by the text.
49067: It opens parables, letters and Gospel scenes in vivid ways, and helps readers see grace, faith and family in their relational setting.
49068: Models can be applied too rigidly, as if all ancient people thought alike. Bailey's use of modern Middle Eastern village life has been questioned as a guide to first-century practice.
49070: Brevard Childs, Christopher Seitz, Kevin Vanhoozer, many Catholic and Orthodox readers
49071: The most important context of any passage is the whole Bible as the church received it. Reconstructed backgrounds help, but they must not replace the canonical text and the faith of the church.
49072: It keeps attention on the text we actually have and on its witness to God, not on speculative reconstructions.
49073: It can neglect history and leave hard cultural questions unanswered, so readers import their own assumptions without noticing.
49075: Greg Boyd, Brad Jersak, Brian Zahnd, Peter Enns, Tommy Miller; in other forms Richard Hays and many Church Fathers
49076: Culture explains how the first hearers understood God's word; Jesus shows what God was always saying through it (Luke 24:27; John 5:39). The last and deepest context of every text is the life, death and resurrection of Jesus.
49077: It keeps background study from becoming mere history and explains why the New Testament reads the Old so freely in light of Christ.
49078: Critics worry it can skip the hard historical work or treat the Old Testament's culture as only an obstacle. Traditional scholars add that the first meaning must still be heard on its own terms before it is seen in Christ.
49080: E. Randolph Richards and Brandon O'Brien (*Misreading Scripture with Western Eyes*); the *Africa Bible Commentary*; the *South Asia Bible Commentary*
49081: Readers from cultures built on honour, extended family and patronage often notice what Western individualist readers miss. Every culture both helps and hinders reading.
49082: It shows that the Western reading is not the neutral one, and it honours the insight of the global church, including Indian and Tamil readers.
49083: It can swap one cultural lens for another — reading modern Asian or African customs into the text is still eisegesis. The ancient world must be studied, not assumed.
49084: "If it is cultural, it does not apply to us"
49085: Some readers fear that once we start explaining passages by their culture, we will explain the Bible away. Others use "that was just their culture" to set aside any command they find difficult.
49086: Context does not remove the message; it locates it. A command given in one culture carries a principle that crosses cultures. Paul himself says the Old Testament was written for our learning (Rom 15:4) and for our admonition (1 Cor 10:11), even though it was first given to Israel.
49087: Traditional evangelical scholars agree that context is essential, but warn against using "culture" as an escape. The real disagreements are over which practices are cultural expressions and which are timeless — for example head coverings (1 Cor 11:5-6) or women teaching (1 Tim 2:12). Scholars on both sides use careful criteria rather than preference.
49088: Without a fair method, people either apply ancient customs rigidly or dismiss whatever is uncomfortable. Both bypass what God was actually saying.
49089: The Prodigal Son is only about one sinner coming home
49090: The parable is usually preached as the story of an individual sinner who wastes his life, repents and comes back to God, who forgives him.
49091: Luke sets the parable in a dispute: religious leaders complained that Jesus welcomed sinners (Luke 15:1-2). The three stories of lost sheep, coin and son build to a story with two lost sons. The older brother, who never left home, stands outside the feast at the end. The father's costly, shame-bearing love reaches out to both.
49092: Traditional scholars agree the older brother is central and the setting is Luke 15:1-2. They also rightly say the younger son's return is a true picture of repentance, so preaching it as a conversion story is a fair application, as long as the older brother is not forgotten.
49093: If the older brother disappears, religious people never hear that the story is also about them. The parable calls insiders as well as outsiders to the Father's feast.
